The ★ fill in z19 is correct: option C, \"But many scientists are taking on this challenge.\", ends with a full stop, and \"their\" in the next sentence refers back to the scientists.

Sentences I checked closely and kept:
z15: \"Helmholtz Center\" (the institute's own name is \"Centre\", but the VOA source uses \"Center\", which fits US spelling). \"plastic wastes\" (acceptable technical plural). The full stop after the closing quote in \"…hard-to-recycle products”.\" is logical punctuation for a quoted fragment, and z17 places it the same way (“Poetry Gathering”.).
z16: No errors found. I looked closely at \"Did you notice how…?\" (acceptable in US English), \"Listening carefully, you will find…\" (the subject \"you\" fits the participle, so it does not dangle), \"it, too, forms\" (commas correctly paired), \"7:00 every morning / 7:30 a.m.\" (acceptable) and \"Just think—without patterns…\".
z17: The serial comma is used in some lists and not others (\"poems, paintings and the rhythm\" vs \"beauty, sweetness, and a smooth feeling\"). notes.grammar:
I compared all five passages against the page images and the full-text dumps; the text matches the printed papers (no transcription differences, paragraph breaks correct). Every finding above is an error in the paper itself.

z15 (Yantai D): Kept: 'plastic wastes' / 'polyurethane-based wastes' (the countable plural 'wastes' for kinds of waste is accepted, technical usage, and Q12 also uses it); 'enzymes that could eat polyurethane' (standard journalistic 'plastic-eating' metaphor); 'a flood of plastics that are ending up' (agreement correct); 'He said that the finding “marks an important step…”' (present tense inside a direct quotation is fine); ', which could be harmful' (a which-clause referring back to the whole act of introducing the bacteria; it is acceptable once 'man-made' is fixed). Possible content slip, not reported: 'made up 3.5 million tons of Europe’s plastics last year'. The VOA source gives this as a 2015 figure, but the passage has no date, so it is not definitely wrong. I could not open the VOA page (proxy blocked); search snippets confirm the bacterium is a naturally occurring soil strain, which supports the 'man-made' finding.

z16 (Henan D): no errors found. Looked closely at: 'Did you notice how nature sometimes repeats itself?' (simple past for a general-experience question is normal American usage; 'Have you noticed' would be the British form, so it is not an error); 'Listening carefully, you will find a noisy world' (the participle's subject is 'you', so it is not dangling); 'Try to find out how living things grow around you' ('around you' = in your surroundings, acceptable); 'So is going to school five days a week and having Saturday and Sunday off' (one combined routine, so singular 'is' is correct); 'it, too, forms a pattern' (must stay, because Q34 asks what 'it' refers to); 'The hotter it is, the more chirps a cricket will make' (correct comparative structure).

z17 (Hubei B): apart from the two findings, kept: 'Besides, they used simple instruments' ('they' comes after 'They' = the cards, but context and the nearer antecedent 'the exchange students' make it clear it means the students); 'By putting poems, paintings and the rhythm together' ('the rhythm' points back to 'the rhythm of the poems'); 'On the cards were famous poems and theme paintings' (inversion with correct plural agreement); 'helped the exchange students know how…'; 'I have to do some closer reading' (present tense inside a quotation); 'not only offer … but also bring' (parallel).

z18 (Hubei C): apart from the adjective-order finding, kept: 'Common people could hardly afford it' (informal 'it' = this service, idiomatic); 'With a small stamp on the cover, people…' (a with + noun + phrase construction, so it is not a dangling modifier); 'a new branch of postal service' ('postal service' used as an uncountable noun is acceptable); 'send packages on festivals' ('during festivals' would be smoother, but 'on' with festival days is acceptable, so I did not report it); 'smart in our life'; 'the moon and other planets' ('other planets' = planets other than Earth, a set phrase); 'Looking forward, will…' (accepted sentence adverbial, like 'Looking ahead'). The 2025 figures are consistent with each other (about 190 billion a year ≈ 6,000 per second ≈ 520 million per day).

z19 (Wuhan C): the filled sentence 'But many scientists are taking on this challenge.' is correct: 'this challenge' picks up 'Exploring the ocean is a really hard job', and 'their' in the next sentence needs 'scientists'. Options A, B and D (from the dump) do not fit, and the sentence is grammatical. 1.4 billion trillion litres = 1.4×10^21, which matches 1,400,000,000,000,000,000,000 and the real ocean volume. Kept: 'where tiny pieces are taken good care of' (the passive of 'take good care of' is grammatical); 'once strong enough, they are planted' (the omitted subject is the pieces, which is also the passive subject, so not dangling); 'They are called “architects” in the ocean'; 'a bag which is connected with an app'; 'To know more about the ocean'; 'Since 1982, scientists have placed…' (present perfect with 'since' is correct). The 'L-shaped Reef' and the 1982 date could not be checked and are not grammar issues.

notes.logic:
I compared all five passages word for word with the rendered page images and the full-text dumps (z15 Yantai D p2, z16 Henan D p1, z17 Hubei B p1, z18 Hubei C p2, z19 Wuhan C p1). Text, paragraph breaks and Chinese glosses all match the paper; I found no transcription errors. The findings above are all errors in the papers themselves.

z15 (plastic-eating bacterium). Source: VOA Learning English, 'Scientists Discover New Bacteria that Feeds on Plastic' (2020); WebFetch could not reach the site, so I used web-search quotes. The quote I relied on: the original says scientists warn against 'man-made enzymes or microorganisms'. The exam's 'the man-made bacteria' therefore contradicts ¶2 ('found the new soil bacterium… found in an area with a lot of plastic wastes'). Kept, with reasons:
- 'plastic wastes' / 'polyurethane-based wastes': the plural 'wastes' is accepted in technical usage (Collins: 'industrial wastes'). The source has 'waste', but this is not wrong.
- 'ending up in the landfills': the article is not needed, but it is not an error.
- 'enzymes that could eat polyurethane': 'plastic-eating enzymes' is standard popular-science wording.
- 'a science magazine': the result actually appeared in the journal Frontiers in Microbiology, but 'magazine' is a tolerable simplification.
- The quote ending '…products”.' with the full stop outside: logical (British) punctuation, acceptable.

z16 (patterns). Source not found. Fact checks:
- Crickets chirp with their wings, and chirp faster in heat: correct (Dolbear's law).
- Honeycomb cells are hexagons: correct.
Kept, with reasons:
- 'Listening carefully, you will find a noisy world': the participle's subject is 'you', so it is not dangling.
- 'So is going to school five days a week and having Saturday and Sunday off': singular, because it is one routine.
- '7:00' then '7:30 a.m.': inconsistent, but not an error.
Only finding: 'Did you notice' (low).

z17 (poetry club). Kept, with reasons:
- 'could be boring': a tentative modal, fine.
- 'Besides,' as a connector: standard.
- 'the rhythm' in the list: refers back to 'the rhythm of the poems'.
- 水 'shows beauty, sweetness…': exam content.
- Facts: Li Bai's moon, Du Fu's mountains, Wang Wei's desert are plausible.

z18 (postal history). Fact checks:
- 1896: the Great Qing Post was established that year, so it is acceptable.
- 2025 express-delivery numbers are mutually consistent. Over 180 billion a year is about 493 million a day and 5,700 a second; the real 2025 total of about 190–200 billion supports 'more than 500 million a day' and 'over 6,000 a second'.
Kept, with reasons:
- 'Common people could hardly afford it': 'it' is vague but understandable.
- 'stamp on the cover': 'cover' is the philatelic term for an envelope.
- 'a new branch of postal service': 'postal service' can be used as a mass noun.
- 'quietest, farthest villages': fine.
- 'There’s no doubt that delivery services are smart in our life…': awkward, but it carries the 'Smarter' idea that Q28 tests, and there is no minimal fix.
- 'Looking forward,': a sentence adverbial, acceptable.

z19 (ocean/coral). Checks on the header's fill and the facts:
- The fill 'But many scientists are taking on this challenge.' is correct and fits: 'their' in the next sentence needs scientists, and 'this challenge' picks up 'a really hard job'. The other options do not fit.
- The number 1,400,000,000,000,000,000,000 = 1.4 × 10^21 litres = 1.4 billion trillion. This is correct and matches the real ocean volume (about 1.33 × 10^21 L).
- 'better maps of Mars than of the ocean floor': a standard NOAA claim.
- 'tiny pieces grow faster': true (microfragmentation).
Kept, with reasons:
- 'L-shaped Reef… Since 1982, scientists have placed old subway cars into the sea': this does not match the real New York subway-car reefs (sunk 2001–2010, Redbird Reef). But 'L-shaped Reef' cannot be found anywhere, so the example seems invented by the exam. I did not report it as a definite error.
- 'To know more about': common and acceptable.
- 'connected with an app' and 'architects in the ocean': acceptable.
Only finding: the missing appositive comma after 'Paul Green'.
